en: The point is that inferential cognition (*anumiti*) is also subsumed under that which is delimited by the property of being counteracted by that [doubt]. Having raised the objection, "How then can there be perceptual doubt from a certainty regarding what possesses the pervaders of both [sides]?"— it is not so.
It indeed exists as long as its invalidity has not been apprehended upon that determination;

thus he says: "And where... By the phrase "non-establishment of the locus, etc.," the non-establishment of the essential nature (*svarūpāsiddhi*) and the non-establishment of the pervasion (*vyāpyatvāsiddhi*) are included.

He refutes the over-extension [of the definition] regarding the non-establishment of the probandum (*sādhyāprasiddhi*) and so forth, with the words: "But as for the non-establishment of the probandum, etc. By the word "etc.," the non-establishment of the probans (*sādhanāprasiddhi*) is included. He states the opinion of certain [scholars] with the words: "In this way, the mountain is fiery, etc. By the phrase "they say," there is a lack of conviction (*asvarasa*); the seed of that [lack of conviction] is as follows:

Since pervasion exists in the case of "blue smoke," how can there be a lack of establishment of being pervaded (*vyāpyatvāsiddhi*)? Nor should it be argued that even though pervasion exists there, because "blueness of smoke" is not a delimiting property (*avacchedaka*), there is indeed a lack of establishment of being pervaded with respect to that [delimitation]. This is because [the definition of] being a delimiting property consists in having a distribution that is not wider [than the property to be delimited].

Because [the property] exists even in the case of "being blue smoke," and because there is an absence of the status of being a delimiting factor (*avacchedakatva*) in the form of an essential relation (*svarūpasambandha*), it is not the case that pervasion (*vyāpyatva*) is unestablished; for if that were so, it would also follow in cases such as "one who possesses a cow is one who possesses a dewlap."

Because it would result in the fallacy of the unestablished nature of the pervasion (*vyāpyatvāsiddhi*). Since the universal such as "cowness" (*gotva*) is simpler than the dewlap and so forth, the dewlap and the like cannot possess the status of a delimiting factor (*avacchedaka*) in the form of an essential relation (*svarūpasambandha*). Or, let it be granted that even in the case of "blue smoke-ness" (*nīladhūmatva*) and the like, there is an absence of such a delimiting factor in the form of an essential relation; therefore, [the pervasion] is not delimited by that.
The non-establishment of pervasion (*vyāpyatvāsiddhi*) consists in the absence of pervasion, but it does not constitute a fallacy of the reason (*hetvābhāsa*),

because it does not contradict the inference nor the cognition of pervasion that serves as its cause. Nor [is there a fallacy] in the case of "that which possesses prameyatva co-located with the mountain, and which is excluded from what is other than fire," by way of co-location with *prameyatva*.

To prevent the undesirable consequence of inference arising from a cognition that apprehends pervasion [only] in a general sense, one must state that the cause of inference is specifically the cognition of pervasion as delimited by the delimitor of the probans-hood (*hetutāvacchedaka*); therefore, the aforementioned "unestablishedness of pervasion" (*vyāpyatvāsiddhi*) is a fallacy of the reason (*hetvābhāsa*) precisely because it is an obstacle to that [cognition].
Even if the cognition of "delimitorhood" (avacchedakatva)— in the sense of not occurring in anything other than that [locus]— is the cause [of the inference],

there is a failure to establish the absence of the object to be apprehended (*grāhyābhāvāsiddhi*) due to the perception of the absence of delimitorhood in the form of an essential relation (*svarūpasaṃbandha*). Thus, the person is defeated by an excess [of qualification].

By the phrase "the absence of the probandum, etc.," there is the inclusion of [the reason's] being other than that which possesses the probandum (*sādhyavadvanya*), as well as its non-existence in the subject (*pakṣāvṛtti*) and so forth. A "certainty regarding the absence of X in a locus Y" (*taddharmikatadabhāvaniścaya*) refers to a certainty regarding the absence of X in locus Y that is non-artificial (*anāhārya*) and not overridden by a cognition of invalidity (*aprāmāṇyajñānānāskandita*).

Since it is an empirical fact that a qualified cognition produced by ordinary sense-contact (*laukika-sannikarṣa*) arises in the moment following a sublating cognition (*bādhaka-buddhi*), he says: "not produced by ordinary sense-contact.

Objection: If this were so, then after a sublating certainty produced by a particular sense-organ, there would follow a qualified cognition of that same object produced by that same sense-organ through ordinary contact. Reply: No, because [the qualification] is non-ordinary (*alaukikatva*).

This is because, without including [the object] within the scope of the delimitor of the state of being obstructed (*pratibadhyatāvacchedaka*), one accepts that a certainty consisting of a non-perceptual (*alaukika*) determination of its absence produced by that sense organ acts as an obstructor toward a qualified cognition (*viśiṣṭabuddhi*) of that [object] produced by that same sense organ.
Following a sublation-determination (*bādhaniścaya*) in the form of a perceptual presentation (*upanītabhāna*) produced by that sense organ...
Because a non-local (alaukika) cognition qualified by that [object] arises from the same sense organ,

"locality" (*laukikatva*) is included within the scope of the delimitor of the counteracting capacity (*pratibandhakatāvacchedaka*). Nor is there [an objection] in the case of a local valid cognition of absence produced by that sense organ regarding its locus.
It should not be argued that because the counter-positive (*pratiyogin*) is non-existent, there is no possibility of a qualified ordinary perception (*laukika-pratyakṣa*) of it,

and thus such a relationship between the sublated (*pratibadhyatva*) and the sublator (*pratibandhakatva*) is unnecessary; for there are cases where the counter-positive exists in its own locus, while the absence in question resides in another proximate locus.

The superimposition consisting of worldly perception is produced by a defect, because subsequently it brings about the worldly perception of the counter-positive (pratiyogin) with respect to that locus;
for in that case, the defect which generates the worldly perception of non-existence acts precisely as an obstacle [to such a perception].
It is not the case that this would lead to the undesirable consequence of the perception of the counter-positive at the very moment the superimposition of the absence arises;
for where there is a superimposition consisting of a worldly perception of absence due to a defect in a state of perishing, immediately thereafter—
Because it brings about the perception of the counter-positive (*pratiyogin*). Where, at the same time as the ordinary valid cognition (*laukika-pramā*) of an absence,

or in its second moment, there occurs in that locus a conjunction of defects that produce an erroneous superimposition (*āropa*) having the counter-positive as its qualifier, there, after the valid cognition of the absence, [the counter-positive appears].

Alternatively, such a relationship between the sublated and the sublator is accepted according to the distinction of the sense organs, in order to prevent the occurrence of superimposition consisting of worldly perception; for instance, even when there is the certainty that "the conch is not yellow" or "the bamboo is not a snake."

To exclude deviation (vyabhicāra) in cases such as the perception of a conch as yellow due to the influence of defects like jaundice (pitamaṇḍūka-vasā-añjana), or the superimposition (āropa) of a bamboo being a snake, he says: "due to a specific defect" (doṣaviśeṣa).
If one were to include the condition of not being produced by a defect in general (doṣasāmānya), then [the definition would apply to] all error (bhrama) whatsoever.

The phrase "therefore, [the term] 'viśeṣa'" is used because otherwise there would be the undesirable consequence that [the cognition] would be sublated. Thus, the meaning is that one must specifically include defects such as jaundice (*kāmalā*), eye-disease (*maṇḍūka-vaśā*), or collyrium (*añjana*) by way of specification, and the state of not being produced by those [defects] must be included within the defining condition (*avacchedaka-koṭi*) for being sublated. This refers to the error [of the form] "it is yellow."

It should not be argued that since the yellowness of the conch-substance is indeed being experienced in its own part, and by accepting its superimposition [upon the shell], it is also "sensory" (laukika) in that part, the exclusion of deviation (*vyabhicāra*) in that case is secured simply by including "non-sensory-ness" (*alaukikatva*) within the delimiting condition (*pratibadhyatāvacchedaka*).
Because even during the state when the father’s substance has not yet reached the conch, the perception of its yellowness arises in the conch and so forth;

therefore, the moderns accept that in this case it is merely a superimposition of what is being remembered, since in that respect it is non-empirical (*alaukika*). This being so, following the perception "the conch is yellow,"...

It is not the case that the apprehension of "immediacy" (sākṣātkāritva) in the cognition "I perceive yellow" is untenable because the ordinary objectivity (*laukika-viṣayatā*) that manifests it is absent there;
for, just like ordinary objectivity, being produced by a specific defect (*doṣa-viśeṣa-janyatva*) is also a manifester of immediacy. Otherwise, [in the case of the illusion] "this is a snake,"...

Thus, since the apprehension of direct perceptuality is untenable in the case of an imposition based on memory, after a subverting cognition produced by that same sense organ— such as "the conch is not yellow"—
there arises, due to defects such as jaundice, an imposition produced by that same sense organ, namely, "the conch is yellow."

If it is established by experience, then it should be noted that even in the previously mentioned relation of the sublated and the sublator—which is differentiated by the diversity of the sense organs—the condition of "not being produced by a specific defect" must be included within the delimiting factor (*avacchedaka*) of sublateness.
Now, one might object: why include "being other than the ordinary" (*laukikānyatva*) within the scope of the delimiting factor for sublateness by sublation?

If it is argued that, upon the ascertainment of a sublation regarding a locus, there would follow a doubt produced by ordinary sensory contact, we say no; for at the time of the arising of an ordinary perception such as "the ground possesses a jar," the absence of a jar— which has somehow been presented independently— does not appear as a qualifier (*prakāra*) with respect to the ground.
To prevent the manifestation of both sides [of a doubt],

it must necessarily be admitted that the worldly perceptual causal complex (*laukika-pratyakṣa-sāmagrī*) regarding one side, when its delimiting property (*dharmitāvacchedaka*) is the same, acts as an inhibitor of the manifestation of the opposite side. And thus...

Even after a certainty of sublation (*bādhaniścaya*), no fault arises; for since the sensory perception-complex (*laukika-pratyakṣa-sāmagrī*) regarding one alternative of that doubt—which is produced by ordinary sense-contact—is present as an inhibitor, the manifestation of the opposite alternative is impossible. If that is so, then where could there ever be a doubt produced by ordinary sense-contact?

If it is argued that [the object] would not appear, we reply: no, because it is possible for the alternative previously presented to appear through the very proximity characterized by cognition (*jñānalakṣaṇāpratyāsatti*). As for the objection that, since the doubt is preceded by [the perception of] those alternatives, and since there exists ordinary sense-contact (*laukikasannikarṣa*) regarding those parts of the alternatives, how could the doubt not be of an ordinary nature?

Or how could there be the manifestation of the contrary alternative (*viparītakoṭi*) in that doubt? [The opponent might argue] that it is because the worldly perceptual causal complex (*laukikapratyakṣasāmagrī*) regarding that alternative—which would be the inhibitor—is present; but that is not so.

For even when ordinary sense-contact (*laukikasannikarṣa*) exists there, the defect (*doṣa*) such as distance (*dūratva*) that generates the doubt and acts as an inhibitor of worldly perception is also present.

"Because of the absence of the causal complex for worldly perception, both [types of cognition] are possible"—thus it is explained at length elsewhere. He refutes the opinion of a certain [author] with the words "But not... This is to be construed with the phrase "this is logical. Now, one might object:

if this is so, then since the absence of the cognition of connection (*saṃsṛṣṭatvajñāna*) itself accounts for the non-occurrence of inference at the time of the ascertainment of sublation (*bādhaniścaya*), [what is the need for further discussion?]

Since a certainty of sublation (*bādhaniścaya*) would not be an obstacle to inference, it would not constitute a fallacy of the reason (*hetvābhāsa*); therefore, he says: "by way of being an obstacle to that. This means: by way of being an obstacle to the cognition of the connection with the probandum (*sādhyasaṃsṛṣṭatvajñāna*), which is the cause of inference.

[Objection: But surely, an inference whose probandum is unestablished never occurs at all; to this he says: "due to doubt regarding the probandum" (*sādhyasaṃśayāt*). [Objection: But even at a time devoid of doubt, there certainly exists a cognition of the connection with the probandum, which consists of a certainty regarding the probandum at the time of the desire to prove (*siṣādhayiṣā*). To this...
He says: "The word 'ādi' (and so forth). By this, the inclusion of an established cognition (*siddhi*) occurring at the time of the desire to prove (*isiṣādhayiṣā*) is intended.
Nor should it be argued that the establishment of inference occurs simply through the arising of another doubt;

for when there is the perception of a distinguishing feature (*viśeṣadarśana*), doubt is impossible. [This applies] in the case of a cognition of the absence of the probandum (*sādhyābhāva*) having the subject (*pakṣa*) as its qualificand.

The certainty of truth (*pramātva-niścaya*) is an obstacle to inference, and its absence is the cause [of inference]; therefore, the ancient view—that such "truth" itself constitutes the sublation (*bādha*)—is refuted with the words "In this way" (*evam*). This means that even the cognition of truth, or even the certainty of truth [is what is meant].

"Because there is no proof" means: because there is no proof for such a cognition—which does not apprehend the absence of the object of apprehension—to be a sublater [of doubt]. "Because there is no proof for such a cognition—which does not apprehend the absence of the object of apprehension—to be a sublater" means: because there is no proof for such a cognition—which does not apprehend the absence of the object of apprehension—to be a sublater. "For such a cognition—which does not apprehend the absence of the object of apprehension—to be a sublater..."

The meaning is "due to the absence of proof. Now, even if there is a cognition of the absence of the probandum (*sādhyābhāva*) in the subject (*pakṣa*), since inference still arises at the time that the invalidity (*aprāmāṇya*) of that cognition is known, the cognition of the absence of the probandum is not an obstacle [to inference].
However, in our view, at that time...

Since the non-arising of inferential cognition occurs precisely because there is no certainty regarding the validity of the knowledge of the absence of the probandum (*sādhyābhāva*), he says: "due to complexity" (*gauravāt*). Thus, in that case, for the sake of accounting for the inferential cognition, it is simply the absence of the knowledge of invalidity (*aprāmāṇyajñāna*)—common to both doubt and certainty—that [is required].

The meaning is that [the certainty of the truth of the cognition] is included within the scope of the delimitors of the obstructive capacity (*pratibandhakatāvacchedaka*), but the obstructive capacity does not consist in the certainty of the truth of the cognition of the absence of the probandum (*sādhyābhāva*) having the subject (*pakṣa*) as its qualificand,
because of the resulting complexity (*gaurava*). This applies where there is a cognition of the absence of the probandum in a given subject, but not otherwise.

The point is that neither the knowledge of validity nor the knowledge of invalidity constitutes an inferential cognition (*anumiti*) in that case. Furthermore, it cannot be argued that its status as a fallacy (*ābhāsa*) is unavoidable because it possesses a pervasion (*anatiriktavṛttitva*) with respect to the obstructiveness of inferential cognition when it has for its object the "truth" (*pramātva*) consisting of a subject (*pakṣa*) that contains the absence of the probandum (*sādhyābhāva*); for [this objection] is like [the case of] "inconstancy" (*vyabhicāra*) qualified by "knowability" (*prameyatva*).
Because it would be impossible for it to be fallacious by virtue of being composed of such other qualified [factors].

Now, if a certainty regarding the absence of the probandum (sādhyābhāva) whose invalidity has not been apprehended were to act as an obstacle [to inference], then a certainty regarding validity, which presents itself first, would likewise be such an obstacle; therefore, he says: "Otherwise... (anyathā).
In the phrase "from a case where the counter-example is real" (*satpratipakṣa*), etc., the word "etc. includes contradiction (*virodha*) and other such fallacies.

Regarding the expression "because of the consequence of being an inhibitor" (*pratibandhakatāpatti*), the phrase "in inference," etc., is to be supplied. Now, [one might object]: "But it is the cognition of the validity (*pramātva*) of the knowledge of the absence of the probandum (*sādhyābhāva*) that constitutes the inhibition of inference; however, in its absence..."
"No," [he says], because the cognition of invalidity acts as an obstacle to inference according to both positive and negative concomitance;
therefore, he says "but rather" (*kiṃtu*). "It is useful in some cases" means that it is so in relation to either the inference itself or the cognition that is its cause.

The meaning is that because it lacks the status of being the object of a cognition that is a direct impediment [to the inference], neither the cognition of the absence of the probandum (*sādhyābhāva*) nor the cognition of either one of them constitutes a fallacious reason (*hetvābhāsa*), since the validity of the cognition of the absence of the probandum lacks the status of being the object of a cognition that is a direct impediment [to the inference].
By the phrase "from the knowledge of deviation, etc.," the inclusion of the knowledge of non-establishment (*asiddhi*) is intended. Regarding the word "due to difference":

thus, even though in a case of sublation (*bādha*) there is a necessary presence of either non-establishment or deviation, the knowledge of sublation is a distinct fallacy of the reason (*hetvābhāsa*), because it lacks the status of having deviation or the like as its object.

[This is] the state of affairs. Nor should it be argued: "Why does the apprehension of sublation (*bādhagraha*) not take the form 'the subject possesses a reason' and 'it possesses the absence of the probandum,' since the causal complex for such an apprehension is present?

And thus, the cognition of sublation would consist merely in a case of deviation (*vyabhicāra*). This is because there exists an obstacle in the form of a non-deviant cognition consisting of the *parāmarśa* (inferential pre-cognition).

Because it is impossible for a sublation-cognition (*bādhabuddhi*) to have deviation (*vyabhicāra*) as its object, and because it is impossible for there to be a certain cognition regarding both deviation and non-deviation in respect to a single probans (*hetu*).
[Objection: But what about the case where fire is the probans and smoke is the probandum, with a red-hot iron ball (*ayogolaka*) as the subject?
Just as there can be a worldly perception of sublation even when there is certainty regarding pervasion (*vyāpti*), so too there could be a worldly perception of deviation (*vyabhicāra*).
To this, he says: "Furthermore" (*kiṃca*). Regarding the phrase "because it is ineffective":
for the cognition of deviation is not a direct obstacle to inference; rather, [it is so only through the production of doubt].

The sense is that, by way of obstructing the *parāmarśa* (the subsumptive reflection), a cognition of deviation (*vyabhicāra*) occurring after the *parāmarśa* is rendered ineffective; thus, in that case, it is the cognition of sublation (*bādhabuddhi*) alone that acts as the obstructor.
He demonstrates sublation even when it is not conflated with deviation and other fallacies, beginning with the words "In this way" (*evam*).
"Of the sublation itself" means that in that case, because the reason exists in the subject (*pakṣa*), there is no "unestablishedness of the essential nature" (*svarūpāsiddhi*);

and because there is an absence of "inconstancy" (*vyabhicāra*)—defined as the property of occurring in a locus where the counter-positive is non-co-located with the absence of the probandum (*sādhya*). This is the intended meaning. Those [reasons] which are distinct from sublation and its pervasions...

The reading is that fallacious reasons (*hetvābhāsa*) and those things pervaded by them (*tadvyāpya*) are included within that very category. Sublation (*bādha*) consists of the subject (*pakṣa*) and so forth as qualified by the absence of the probandum (*sādhyābhāva*);

its pervaded form is the counter-balanced reason (*satpratipakṣa*). Those distinct from it—namely, the inconclusive (*vyabhicāra*), the contradictory (*viruddha*), and the unestablished (*asiddha*)—along with their pervaded forms, are included therein.

This is the meaning. Just as with [the fallacies of] *vyabhicāra* (inconstancy) and so forth, since *vyabhicāravyāpya* (that which is pervaded by inconstancy) is also an object of a cognition that obstructs the apprehension of pervasion (*vyāpti*), it would follow that it is not included among the five standard fallacious reasons (*hetvābhāsa*) and would thus constitute an additional, distinct fallacy. [The phrase] "it is not an obstructor" [is used].

The sense is that there is no evidence for the claim that the cognition of something possessing a pervader of the absence of the probandum (sādhyābhāvavyāpyavyāpyavatā) is opposed to the cognition of the presence of the probandum (sādhyavatā). || 71 || 72 || Regarding the phrase "due to the difference in the seeds of their being defeaters": [this refers to] the case where the common [inconclusive reason] prevents the cognition of non-deviation, and the contradictory [reason] prevents the apprehension of co-presence (sāmānādhikaraṇya).

The sense is that [it is] because of being an obstacle. He states—“as for the co-subject” (sapakṣa)—that the status of being a co-subject, which constitutes the factor of "uniqueness" (asādhāraṇya), contains a certainty within it, and not merely the state of possessing the probandum (sādhyavatva). The same applies hereafter.
He states the result of including certainty in the definitions of being a co-subject and being a counter-subject (vipakṣa) with the words beginning “sound,” etc.

"Previously stated" means it was stated in the passage beginning with "the uncommon [reason] is that which does not have the same locus as the probandum," and so forth. (73) Regarding the phrase "having a purely positive subject": here, "subjecthood" (*pakṣatā*) is understood in the form of doubt regarding the probandum; therefore, [in the case of the argument] "everything is nameable,"...

In cases such as "because of being an object of cognition" (*prameyatvāt*), when there is both proof (*siddhi*) and the desire to prove (*siṣādhayiṣā*), the certainty of the probandum (*sādhyaniścaya*) is possible; consequently, since the apprehension of pervasion (*vyāptigraha*)—which is constituted by co-location (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*)—is possible, that [reason] is not to be characterized as a valid reason (*saddhetu*). Therefore, [the definition of a valid reason must be] qualified by the absence of proof qualified by the absence of the desire to prove (*siṣādhayiṣāvirahaviśiṣṭasiddhyabhāvaviśiṣṭa*).
In that case, even though the subject (*pakṣa*) is purely positively concomitant (*kevalānvayin*), there is no over-extension (*ativyāpti*) [of the definition] to it.
He establishes the status of the non-conclusive (*anupasaṃhārī*) as a fallacious reason (*hetvābhāsa*) with the words beginning "everything is nameable" (*sarvam abhidheyam*).

Because there is no other instance where co-referentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) is apprehended. Since it must necessarily be stated that the causal complex for doubt (*saṃśaya-sāmagrī*) acts as an inhibitor with respect to certainty (*niścaya*) in order to prevent certainty from arising at the very moment a doubt occurs, [this applies] in the present case wherever there is doubt regarding the probandum (*sādhya*).

The point is this: since it is impossible for there to be a certainty regarding the probandum (sādhya) anywhere prior to that [inference]—given the existence of the causal complex [for such a certainty]—the apprehension of pervasion (vyāpti), in the form of the cognizability (prameyatva) qualified by the co-location (sāmānādhikaraṇya) with the pervading probandum, cannot arise; therefore, no inference occurs therein, which is why the inconclusive (anupasaṃhārī) reason is considered a fallacious reason (hetvābhāsa).
The meaning is that there is no harm [to the definition] even now because of the absence of such damage;
that is, there is no harm to the status of being a "kevalānvayi" (purely positive) subject or to the status of being "anupasaṃhārī" (non-conclusive).

And thus, since non-conclusiveness exists in that case, and since it lacks the capacity to cause the non-arising of the cognition of pervasion (*vyāpti*), its classification as a fallacy of the reason (*hetvābhāsa*) is untenable.
This is the state of affairs. Nor should it be asked: "Since the causal complex for doubt exists, how can there be certainty regarding the probandum in one part of the subject?
For even when the causal complex for doubt exists with respect to the entire property that delimits the subjecthood (*dharmitāvacchedaka*), [certainty may still arise].

Because there is no obstacle to the production of a certainty regarding the probandum (sādhya) when the delimiting property of the subject (dharmitāvacchedaka)—such as "pot-ness"—is present, since contradiction occurs only through having the same mode of presentation (samānaprakārakatva). Even if [the opponent] maintains that sublation is an impediment by virtue of having the same object (samānaviṣayakatva), he says: "Or let it be so," etc. "Of that" refers to the non-apprehension of concomitance (sahacāra). Of that...

The point is that since only that which exists in its own right (*svarūpasat*) constitutes a contradiction, the cognition of such a thing lacks the capacity to be the cause for the non-arising of an inference. Nor is it the case that doubt itself— serving as the cause for the failure to grasp the concomitance (*sahacāra*) with that [reason]— is the fallacious reason (*hetvābhāsa*), for that too...

Because only that which exists in its own right (*svarūpasat*) can be contradictory. Nor should it be argued that the object of doubt—the subject (*pakṣa*) qualified by the absence of the probandum (*sādhyābhāva*)—is itself a fallacy (*ābhāsa*) in that context;
for in cases such as "everything is nameable" (*sarvam abhidheyam*), the subject qualified by the absence of nameability is unestablished (*aprasiddha*). This has been discussed elsewhere.

The detailed explanation follows. Regarding the phrase "for that purpose": the intention is that there is no over-extension (*ativyāpti*) to the uncommon [probans] by means of that [definition]. || 74 || Regarding the phrase "the nature of the prior absence of smoke" (*dhūmaprāgabhāvatva*):

since that [prior absence] is composed of the property of being smoke (*dhūmatva*), which serves as the delimiting factor of pervasion (*vyāpyatāvacchedaka*), it would not be included [by the definition].

[The definition of the probans] is: being an entity that is not non-composite with itself, where "non-composition with itself" consists in not being the object of a cognition that does not have itself as its object.

[Objection: One might argue that even "blue-smokeness" (nīladhūmatva) is indeed non-composite with such another property, because "smokeness" (dhūmatva) is not distinct from "blue-smokeness. [Response: This should not be said.

Because the meaning of that [term] is defined as being the object of a cognition in which it is not itself the object, which amounts to its not being the locus of the subsistence of the delimitation that is determined by the mode-determination (prakāratā) whose delimitation is in turn determined by a delimitation that is resident in itself.

This is because there is no difference between the property-ness whose delimitation is pervaded by the pure smoke-ness (*śuddhadhūmatva*) and the property-ness whose delimitation is pervaded by smoke-ness as qualified by blueness (*nīlatva*), and so forth. Now, one might object: "In this case, it would be untenable for the property of 'not being excluded from what is other than fire' (*vahnimadanyāvṛttitva*) to be the delimitor of the pervasion of fire (*vahnivyāpyatāvacchedakatā*), since that property is composed of fire-ness (*vahnitva*) and another such property."

If it is argued that this is not so, because it is impossible to intend for another property to be non-constitutive as a qualifier due to the fear that properties such as "being different from smoke" would result in being the delimitors of pervasion (*vyāpyatāvacchedaka*), we say no;
for by the phrase "co-located with itself" (*svasamānādhikaraṇa*), what is intended is "pervaded by itself" (*svavyāpakatva*).

Because the state of being "other than a non-fire" (anagny-anya) does not pervade the state of being "other than a non-smoke" (adhūmānyāvṛttitva), and because the state of being smoke (dhūmatva) does pervade the state of being "other than what is other than smoke" (dhūmānyānyatva), the aforementioned defects do not arise. Furthermore, the pervasion of a different property [by the reason] occurs by virtue of that property being a delimiting factor for the relation to the probandum (sādhya-sambandhitāvacchedaka) within its own constituents; otherwise, [the pervasion would fail] in the case of "being either smoke or light" (dhūmālokānyataratva).

[Otherwise,] there would be the undesirable consequence (*āpatti*) that *dhūmatva* (smokiness) and *ālokātva* (luminosity) would each be a delimiting factor (*avacchedaka*) for the non-pervasion (*avyāpti*) of "being one or the other" (*anyataratva*),

because each of them individually does not pervade "being one or the other. [In the phrase] "upon the consideration (*parāmarśa*) of two contradictory reasons," [the intended meaning is] "the consideration of two contradictory reasons."

To ward off this misconception, he says: "svasādhyeti" (his own probandum). This means: "sva" refers to the reason intended as a counter-balanced opponent (*satpratipakṣa*); that which is contrary to its probandum is the absence of the probandum (*sādhyābhāva*).
Now, an objection: the statement in the original text, "the jar at the time of its production," etc., is improper, because in that case, the jar is the subject (*pakṣa*).

Because there is no absence of the emptiness of odor, he says: "by the delimiting condition of the subject" (*pakṣatāvacchedaka*). To avoid the deficiency of the root text—which would arise because a contradiction (*bādha*) is possible even if space, like time, were to serve as the delimiting condition of the subject—he says: "in this way. [The word] "is to be understood" (*bodhyam*) refers to that [property] in the subject, namely, the tree.

The meaning is that even though conjunction exists [in general], there is an absence of conjunction at the specific locus delimited by the *pakṣatāvacchedaka* (the delimitor of the subject). || 75 || 76 || 77 || 78 || Thus ends the section on Inference (*anumāna-khaṇḍa*) in the *Muktāvalīprakāśa*, composed by Mahādevabhaṭṭa, son of Bālakṛṣṇabhaṭṭa, who is like the full moon in the ocean of the illustrious Bhāradvāja lineage.
Intending to establish the logical connection (*saṅgati*) with the present context, he says: "the cognition of similarity" (*upamitim*).

Therein, in the case of the *gavaya*, the "perception of similarity" (*sādṛśyadarśana*) is the direct perception of similarity. That is the instrument (*karaṇa*) of that analogical cognition (*upamiti*).
This is according to the view of the Neo-Nyāya (*navīna*) school. [According to others,] it is the verbal comprehension (*śābdabodha*) of the meaning of the instructional statement (*atideśavākya*).

The traditional view holds that the instrument (*karaṇa*) is the recollection of the meaning of the analogical statement (*atideśavākya*), while the operation (*vyāpāra*) is the perception of the object (*piṇḍa*) as qualified by similarity, which acts as a cooperative factor (*sahakārī*). However, since the perception of the object as qualified by similarity is necessarily required as a cooperative factor, it is that very perception which constitutes the instrument.
The phrase "it is logical" has been set aside. As for the statement "the memory that arises":

the meaning is that the perception of an object qualified by similarity acts as a stimulus (*udbodhaka*) and thereby causes the recollection of the meaning of such a sentence. That [recollection] itself is the operation (*vyāpāra*).

By this [it is shown that] in a case where, following the perception of an individual object qualified by similarity, there arises the cognition of the meaning of the analogical statement (*atideśavākya*), the perception of the individual object qualified by similarity is not the instrument (*karaṇa*) having the recollection of the meaning of the analogical statement as its mediating operation (*vyāpāra*); rather, the mere cognition of similarity is the instrument.

The view of some— that the two factors, namely the knowledge of the meaning of the analogical statement (*atideśavākya*) produced by the cognition of the qualifier, and the perception of the individual object (*piṇḍadarśana*) as qualified by similarity, constitute the operation (*vyāpāra*)—
is refuted. In which [case]...

The sense is that, since verbal cognition of the meaning of the analogical statement (*atideśavākya*) following the perception of an individual object qualified by similarity is not admitted as being "analogy" (*upamiti*),
rather, after that [verbal cognition], there occurs again the perception of the individual object qualified by similarity,
from which follows the recollection of the meaning of the analogical statement, and immediately after that, analogy itself arises.

Regarding the cognition that arises— "The gavaya is denotable by the word 'gavaya'"— this is not a distinct means of valid knowledge (pramiti), but rather consists of verbal comprehension (śābdabodha). This is because, in the statement "the gavaya is similar to a cow," there occurs the apprehension of the denotability of the word "gavaya" as delimited by the similarity presented by the word "similar."
The view that the nature of analogy (*upamiti*) consists solely in the form "the *gavaya* is denotable by the word 'gavaya' because it resembles a cow" is refuted;

for an analogy whose object is the denotability of the word 'gavaya' as delimited by *gavaya*-ness cannot exist without the presentation of the *gavaya* as qualified by *gavaya*-ness, which is produced by the word 'gavaya'.

This is because it is impossible for [the cognition] to be of the nature of verbal comprehension (*śābdabodha*). Nor should it be argued: "Since both the similarity to a cow and the property of being a *gavaya* are presented through perception, why does the analogical inference (*upamiti*) result in the denotability of the word 'gavaya' as restricted precisely by the property of being a *gavaya*, and not by the restriction of similarity?"

Even though there is an apprehension of similarity, because the cognition of the greater complexity (*gaurava*) of cow-similarity relative to the genus *gavayatva* prevents the arising of an analogical inference (*upamiti*) regarding the denotability of the word "gavaya" as delimited by that [similarity], and because a verbal cognition (*śābdabodha*) having *gavayatva* as its qualifier would otherwise be untenable from the word "gavaya," [the following is required] for a verbal cognition having that as its qualifier:

Because the apprehension of the word’s denotative power (*śaktigraha*) has as its cause the cognition of similarity delimited by that [specific property]. Nor is it the case that, because an inferential cognition (*upamiti*) of the denotability of the word "gavaya" delimited by *gavayatva* does not arise from a cognition of similarity in respect of what is qualified by substantiality (*dravyatva*), the cognition of similarity must reside in that which is qualified by that specific property (*taddharma*).

It must be stated that [the cognition] which produces the analogy does so by means of the delimitation of that property (*taddharmāvacchedena*). And thus, when the universal such as "gavaya-ness" (*gavayatva*) is not present, since similarity is apprehended as qualified by heavy properties such as configuration (*saṃsthāna*) and the like, it is by means of that [delimitation].

It should not be argued that this results in the undesirable consequence of [the cognition] being an analogy (upamiti) regarding the denotability of the word "gavaya" and so forth; for such a consequence is accepted.

This is because, being an error (*bhrama*), it does not establish the denotability of the word "gavaya" and so forth with respect to such a cumbersome property (*gurudharma*) as its delimiting condition (*avacchedaka*). This [point] is merely illustrative.

It should also be understood that the instrument (*karaṇa*) is the perception of an individual object qualified by its dissimilarity [to others]; the operation (*vyāpāra*) is the recollection of the meaning of the analogical statement (*atideśavākya*), namely, "Earth possesses qualities dissimilar to those of water and so forth";
and the result (*phala*) is the analogical cognition (*upamiti*) of the denotability of the word "earth" as delimited by earthness (*pṛthivītva*). Now, regarding analogy (*upamāna*)...

There is no evidence for its being a distinct means of valid cognition (*pramāṇāntara*). Nor can it be argued that it is a distinct means of valid cognition because it is the instrument of a cognition of a different class from perceptions and other cognitions, since comparison (*upamiti*) lacks such a difference in class from perception and other cognitions—if you say this, we reply: no.

Since comparison (upamiti) arises even when the operation of the eyes and other senses has ceased, it cannot be visual (cākṣuṣa) or the like; nor can it be mental (mānasa), because the cognition "I am comparing" does not arise immediately after a mental perception, as its object is the content of comparison. Immediately following comparison, one has the experience "I am directly perceiving."

Furthermore, there is no evidence for its being perception, because perception does not arise [in that case]; otherwise, even inference would have to be considered mental perception. Nor is it inference, because it arises even without the knowledge of pervasion (*vyāpti*) and so forth. It is not verbal cognition, because it is not produced by the knowledge of words. Nor...
Memory [is established] because it is impossible to remember an object that has not been previously experienced; this is the summary. || 79 || 80 ||

Thus ends the section on Analogy (*upamāna*) in the *Muktāvalīprakāśa*, composed by Mahādevabhaṭṭa, the son of Bālakṛṣṇabhaṭṭa, who is the full moon in the ocean of the lineage of the venerable Bhāradvāja.
Intending to establish the logical connection based on the relationship between that which is depended upon and that which depends, he says:
"In the root [text], however, it is the knowledge of the word. He clarifies what is excluded by the word *tu* (however) located in the root—which carries the sense of the particle *eva*—by stating:
"In the Muktāvalī, however, it is not the word as being known (*jñāyamāna*)."

By the phrase "in the case of Mauni’s verse and so forth," there is an inclusion of non-linguistic hand gestures and the like that convey duality and other such meanings; otherwise, if the mere cognition of the word-meaning were the operation (*vyāpāra*), then even in that case— namely, even when there is the presentation of the word-meaning produced by the words— [the objection would remain].
The meaning of the locative case [in "vṛttau"] is "container-ness" (ghaṭakatva). Otherwise, if the word "vṛtti" were not included, [the definition would be incomplete]. Now, an objection:

if "vṛtti" means "denotative power" (śakti), then there would be no cognition of the bank and so forth from the word "Gaṅgā," because in that case there would be no presentation of the bank produced by the word through denotative power; therefore, he says: "And vṛtti... [meaning it includes both denotative power and secondary indication].

"Connection with either" means a connection consisting of either one [of the two]. "In this very [case]" means precisely in the case of the presentation of the word-meaning generated by the word. Regarding the phrase "and that": although the will of God (*īśvarecchā*) is unitary, there is the divine will that "from the word 'jar,' a jar is to be understood."

If it were argued that [the desire] exists even in the cloth, there would be the fallacy of over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*). Likewise, since the desire whose qualifier is "being the object of the cognition produced by the word *gaṅgā*" exists in the bank as well, the cognition of the bank could be accounted for through primary denotation (*śakti*) alone; thus, there would be the undesirable consequence of the abolition of figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*). Nevertheless, regarding the conventional usage of the term "denoted by the word *gaṅgā*":

The denotative power (*śakti*) of words such as "Ganges" resides in God's will (*īśvarecchā*), related to the bank by way of a qualificandhood (*viśeṣyatā*) determined by a subjecthood (*prakāratā*) delimited by the property of being the object of a cognition produced by the word "Ganges. Although the qualificandhood residing in the bank is indeed determined by the subjecthood of being the object of a cognition produced by the word "Ganges," [the power does not reside there].

Its being determined by such a mode-of-apprehension (prakāratā) is due to its being a [specific] objective-relation (viṣayatā) of that kind, but it is rather due to its being a pure objective-relation; thus there is neither over-extension nor the collapse of the definition.
Regarding a modern name, [it is given] on the eleventh day by modern fathers and others.
"In a conventional name" means "by the will of the Lord";
that is to say, in its general form as a name that is the object of a father's utterance on the eleventh day. However, in the case of a name assigned by a modern convention...

Regarding words such as *nadīvṛddhi* (the rising of a river), which are designated by purely modern convention, the author sets aside the lack of elegance in the traditional view held in his heart and presents the new school’s position, beginning with "The moderns, however. He states, "It is not [a matter of] denotative power (*śakti*). For if that were the case, there would be no verbal cognition (*śābdabodha*) arising from words like *nadi* and so forth when they are designated by modern convention.

The sense is that [the word] would not [denote its meaning]. It should be noted that in both views, the comprehension [of meaning] from corrupt words such as *gargari* arises solely due to a misconception of their expressive power (*śakti*). "From grammar" means from grammatical rules such as "the root *bhū* is used in the sense of existence" and "the suffix *laṭ* [is used] in the present tense. "Due to parsimony" (*lāghavāt*)...

The meaning is that there is parsimony (*lāghava*) in taking the universal *kṛtitva* (the nature of being an agent) as the delimiting factor of denotability (*śakyatāvacchedaka*). And [it is said] "because the agent is not expressed" (*anabhidhānāt*); this is because, under the governing rule (*adhikāra*) "when not already expressed" (*anabhihite*), the rule "the third case ending is used for the agent and the instrument" (*kartṛkaraṇayos tṛtīyā*) prescribes the third case ending for an unexpressed agent.

The state [of being]. In that regard, [it occurs] in the third [case], because of its being the governing factor (*tantra*) and the motivator (*prayojaka*). Now, raising the objection as to what exactly is the motivator for the denotation of the agent’s number, he shows that motivator with the words "denotation of number" (*saṃkhyābhidhāna*). In examples such as *caitraḥ pacati taṇḍulān* ("Caitra cooks rice"), [the verb denotes the number].

In order to exclude *taṇḍula* and other entities presented by nominative words that are characterized by [grammatical roles] such as objecthood (*karmatva*), he says: "not already occupied by objecthood and so forth" (*karmatvādyanavaruddha*).
Now, one might object: in a sentence such as *caitra iva maitro gacchati*, since [the number] in the form of the singular number has been expressed by the verb (*ākhyāta*)...
Furthermore, the number would have to be construed with *caitra*, because it is not already occupied by [the relation of] being the object (*karman*) and so forth,

and because it is presented by a word ending in the nominative case. Moreover, in expressions such as "cooked rice is eaten" (*pakkam annaṃ bhujyate*), the construction of the number with the rice and so forth would be untenable, since the status of being the object of cooking (*pākakarman*) is already construed with the rice.

Because there is no absence of being unexcluded by "objectness" (*karmatva*) and so forth, he says: "of the term 'objectness,' etc. Thus, the word "objectness" refers to the others, and "unexcluded" means not intended as a qualifier.
In reality, however, even the others are not intended, because what is intended is merely the state of not being a qualifier.

The state of being non-qualifying (*aviśeṣaṇatva*) consists in being devoid of being a mode (*prakāratā*). Since this [state] exists even in Caitra and others prior to the verbal cognition, there would be the undesirable consequence (*āpatti*) of number (*saṃkhyā*) being construed with Caitra as well in sentences such as "Maitra goes just like Caitra. Nor is it the case that [the state of being non-qualifying] belongs to Caitra...

It must be asked: since the understanding of the subordinate sentence-meaning "similarity" exists prior [to the main sentence], how can Caitra not be a qualifier? [The answer is: In cases where the understanding occurs according to the "pigeons on a threshing floor" maxim (*khalekapotanyāya*), there is no prior understanding of the subordinate sentence-meaning "the similarity belonging to Caitra"; therefore...

The pursuit [of the definition] extends as far as being a qualifier (*viśeṣaṇatva*) and not being the intended object of emphasis (*tātparyāviṣayatva*). Nor should it be argued: "In cases such as *caitra eva pacati* ('Caitra alone cooks') or *caitraścaitraṃ paśyati* ('Caitra sees Caitra'), since Caitra is a qualifier of the meaning of the particle *eva* (i.e., exclusion) and of the other [factors] such as the object, how can number be construed there? [This objection does not hold.]
This is because what is intended is simply the state of being a qualifier (*viśeṣaṇatva*) while not being the object of the speaker's primary intention (*tātparya*).

In the case mentioned, Caitra possesses both the state of being a qualifier and the state of being the primary qualificand (*mukhyaviśeṣyatva*), and thus he is the object of the primary intention; consequently, the connection with number is logically established there. Furthermore, in cases such as "Maitra is like Caitra,"...

When Caitra and others do not function as qualifiers, then there would be the unwanted consequence of the number [of the verb] applying to Caitra as well. Nor should it be argued that this is not the case because the knowledge of the speaker’s intention (*tātparya-jñāna*) is a cause for verbal cognition.
